info.title: BirdNet-Behavior HTTP API
info.summary: JSON API for a BirdNet-Behavior acoustic monitoring station: open read-only endpoints, plus a small token-authenticated write surface.
info.description:
Everything the dashboard shows is backed by this versioned API under `/api/v2`. Almost every endpoint is a read-only `GET`; the exceptions are the four `/detections/*` write endpoints, which require a bearer token.

**Authentication.** The read-only endpoints, the WebSocket stream and the health check are intentionally open to anyone who can reach the port — restrict them at the network layer (VPN / reverse-proxy allow-list) if that matters. This is by design, not a bug.

The **write** endpoints are different: each requires `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, where the token is the station's `BNB_API_TOKEN`. A station that has not been given one answers `404` on every write endpoint — the write surface does not exist until an operator enables it, and it is never covered by the `/admin` password's open-when-unset behaviour. Generate a token with `openssl rand -base64 48`; anything shorter than 32 bytes is refused and leaves the write surface off.

**Not described here.** A live detection WebSocket stream at `ws://<host>/api/v2/ws/detections`, the live audio stream at `/stream`, RSS/iCal feeds under `/feeds/*`, and per-detection public share pages under `/r/{token}` are part of the surface but are not GET-JSON endpoints; see the project docs.

**Analytics.** The `/analytics/*` and `/timeseries/*` families are powered by the bundled DuckDB engine, which is on by default. When it is disabled (or not compiled in), those endpoints answer `200` with a body of `{"status":"unavailable",...}` rather than failing.

**Base URL.** A `GET` to the API root (`/api/v2`, no trailing slash) returns the API name, version and status.

get.description: The machine-readable description of this API (this very document).

Use for monitoring. `status` is `healthy` (HTTP 200) or `degraded` (HTTP 503), so an alert can key on the status code alone.

Without `strict`, only a database that is unreachable or has a recorded failed integrity check is degraded. This is the right answer for a container health check: Docker restarts an unhealthy container, and a station whose detection daemon is down is exactly the one that must stay up to be diagnosed.

With `strict`, a stopped detection daemon is degraded too. Point a pager at this form — otherwise a station that has recorded nothing for months answers 200.

503.description: Station is degraded (database integrity check failed).

parameters.name: strict
parameters.description: Also report 503 when the detection daemon is not running. Accepts an empty value, `1`, `true`, `yes` or `on`.

post.summary: Apply one operation to many detections
post.description:
One round trip, one authentication and one result document instead of N of each — what a triage client rejecting forty overnight false positives needs.

**This is not a transaction.** Each detection goes through the same code path as the single-detection endpoint, so the SQLite store and the DuckDB analytics copy stay in step; one shared transaction would mean a second implementation of "delete a detection" and is not worth that. A key that matches nothing does not stop the batch either: a client working from a slightly stale list would otherwise have forty good deletions refused because three rows had already gone.

**Read `failed`, not just the status code.** The response is `200` whenever the request itself was well-formed, even if every item failed — the request was understood and carried out, and the per-item outcomes are the body. `applied` and `failed` are at the top level so a caller need not walk `results` to know what happened.

Every detection actually changed is written to the station's audit log individually, under the same action name the single-detection endpoint uses, so "what happened to that recording?" stays answerable. A full batch of 500 writes 500 audit rows, which is one page of the station's audit view.

op.description: Applied to every detection in the list. An unrecognised value is refused rather than ignored.

status.description: `review` only; omit to clear an existing verdict. Sending it with any other `op` is a `400`, because a caller who wrote it believes it did something.

notes.description: `review` only; attached to every verdict in the batch.

detections.description: At most 500 per request; a longer list is refused before anything is written rather than truncated.

date.description: Local calendar date of the detection, `YYYY-MM-DD`.

sci_name.description: Scientific name exactly as the detection was recorded.

com_name.description: Read only when `op` is `review`; defaults to `sci_name`.

200.description: The request was carried out. Check `failed` — this is also the status when every item failed.

failed.description: How many were not — malformed key, no such detection, or a database error.

results.description: One entry per detection, in the order sent.

400.description: An unknown `op`, `status`/`notes` on a non-review `op`, an unparseable verdict, or more than 500 detections.

401.description: No `Authorization: Bearer` header, or the token does not match.

404.description: This station has no `BNB_API_TOKEN`, so the write surface does not exist.

get.description:
Every persisted setting, with credentials removed two ways: by key name (`email_smtp_pass`, `birdweather_token`) and by value shape, which catches the credential inside a URL such as `ntfy://user:pass@host`. The by-shape rules are blunt: that value comes back as `***@host`, keeping the host and path but not the scheme or username, so a redacted value is not one you can edit and send back. A redacted value is **replaced** with `***REDACTED***` rather than omitted, so a caller can tell a secret it may not read from a setting that was never configured; `redacted` lists exactly which keys those were.

Known gap: a URL whose *path segment* is the credential — a heartbeat ping URL, for instance — is caught by neither rule and is returned in full.

settings.description: Every persisted key, in sorted order.

redacted.description: The keys whose value was replaced with `***REDACTED***`.

401.description: No `Authorization: Bearer` header, or the token does not match.

404.description: This station has no `BNB_API_TOKEN`, so the settings API does not exist.

put.description:
A partial update: send only the keys you mean to change. Values may be strings, numbers or booleans; each is stored as the string the settings table holds, through the same normalisation the admin page uses (so `"51,5"` is stored as `51.5`). A key already holding the value sent is not rewritten and is not counted in `updated`.

Unknown keys are refused rather than ignored — a misspelling that answered 200 would report a change that never happened — and so is the literal `***REDACTED***`, which is what a client gets back from `GET /settings` for a secret and must not write over the real value.

The change is recorded in the station's audit log by key name only, never by value.

schema.description: Setting keys to values. Keys must come from `writable_keys`.

200.description: The settings were written. `updated` is 0 when every value already matched.

400.description: An unknown key, a value with no string form, the `***REDACTED***` placeholder, or a body that is not a JSON object.

401.description: No `Authorization: Bearer` header, or the token does not match.

404.description: This station has no `BNB_API_TOKEN`, so the settings API does not exist.

post.description:
Sends this process `SIGTERM` after a short delay, so the response is written before the socket closes; systemd's `Restart=always` brings a fresh instance up. The request body is ignored.

Answers `503` when the process is not running under systemd, because nothing would then bring the station back — a `200` there would tell the caller the opposite of what is about to happen. The attempt is recorded in the audit log either way.

200.description: `SIGTERM` sent; systemd will start a fresh instance.

401.description: No `Authorization: Bearer` header, or the token does not match.

404.description: This station has no `BNB_API_TOKEN`, so the control API does not exist.

503.description: Not running under systemd, so nothing would restart the process. Nothing was signalled.

bearerAuth.description: The station's `BNB_API_TOKEN`, resolved from its configuration file and then its environment. Required by every write endpoint, and by the settings read — a station's configuration is not public even with its credentials taken out. The read-only detection, species and analytics endpoints accept no credential and ignore one if it is sent.

Species.description: Filter to one species (common or scientific name).

Days.name: days
Days.description: How many days back to include.

MaxGap.description: Maximum gap, minutes, between steps in a sequence.

HourStart.name: hour_start
HourStart.description: Restrict to detections at or after this hour (0-23).

HourEnd.name: hour_end
HourEnd.description: Restrict to detections before this hour (0-23).

Filename.name: filename
Filename.description: Recording filename (basename only; no path separators or `..`).

AnalyticsResult.description: Analytics result. The exact shape depends on the endpoint; each carries a top-level array of rows plus a `total` count. When the analytics engine is disabled the body is `{"status":"unavailable"}` instead.

schema.description: Endpoint-specific result rows plus counts, or an unavailability marker.

detection_silence_secs.description: Seconds since the most recent stored detection, or null before the first measurement.

strict.description: Which mode this response answered in.

EngineStatus.description: Availability of an optional engine, plus the endpoints it serves.

DetectionRow.description: One detection. Optional fields are omitted when unknown (historical / imported rows).

duration_secs.description: Length of the saved clip in seconds.
